title: Free fall: vertical motion under gravity
summary: Drop a stone or toss a ball straight up — once it leaves your hand without air drag, its acceleration is always g = 9.8 m/s² downward, even at the peak.

u.label: $u$
u.meaning: initial vertical velocity at launch (t = 0), in m/s
u.body: Positive when thrown upward (if up is positive), zero when dropped from rest, and negative when thrown downward.
u.example: Tossing a ball straight up at $u = +19.6\text{ m/s}$.
u.analogy: The launch kick your hand gives the ball right before letting go.

g.label: $g$
g.meaning: gravitational acceleration near Earth, 9.8 m/s² downward
g.body: Every object in {free_fall|free fall} shares this exact same downward acceleration regardless of mass. With upward chosen as positive, $a = -g = -9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.
g.example: Each second of flight shifts vertical velocity by $-9.8\text{ m/s}$.
g.analogy: An invisible hand pulling downward at the exact same pace on every flying object.

v_top.label: $v_{\text{top}} = 0$
v_top.meaning: instantaneous velocity at the highest point, in m/s
v_top.body: At the peak, upward motion finishes and downward motion begins, so velocity passes through **zero** — while acceleration stays $g$ downward.
v_top.example: Setting $v = 0$ in $v = u - gt$ immediately gives the climb time.
v_top.analogy: The split-second pause of a swing at the top of its arc before swinging back.

h_max.label: $h_{\max}$
h_max.meaning: maximum height reached above the launch point, in meters
h_max.body: Equal to $u^2 / (2g)$. Doubling the launch speed quadruples the peak height!
h_max.example: Launched at $u = 19.6\text{ m/s}$ with $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$, the ball reaches $h_{\max} = 19.6\text{ m}$.
h_max.analogy: The highest mark the ball paints on a tall measuring wall.

t_up.label: $t_{\text{up}}$
t_up.meaning: time taken to climb from launch to the highest point, in seconds
t_up.body: Found from $0 = u - g t_{\text{up}}$, so $t_{\text{up}} = u / g$.
t_up.example: With $u = 19.6\text{ m/s}$ and $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$, the climb takes $t_{\text{up}} = 2\text{ s}$.
t_up.analogy: Half of a symmetrical round-trip flight.

t_total.label: $T$
t_total.meaning: total flight time until returning to the launch height, in seconds
t_total.body: Without air resistance, the trip down mirrors the trip up, so $T = 2t_{\text{up}} = 2u/g$.
t_total.example: Climbing for $2\text{ s}$ and falling for $2\text{ s}$ gives $T = 4\text{ s}$.
t_total.analogy: The total hang time between toss and catch at the same hand height.

no_air.label: no air drag
no_air.meaning: air resistance is negligible, so gravity is the only force
no_air.body: Keeps vertical acceleration strictly constant at $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$, allowing all {suvat|uniform acceleration equations} and {symmetry|up-and-down symmetry} to hold.
no_air.example: A dense stone tossed a few meters behaves almost identically to vacuum free fall; a sheet of paper does not.
no_air.analogy: Dropping objects inside a vacuum tube.

top_trap.title: At the top: v = 0, but a ≠ 0
top_trap.body: Students often think [g:acceleration] drops to zero at the highest point because [v_top:velocity is zero]. If $a$ were zero when $v = 0$, the ball would hover in mid-air forever! Gravity pulls continuously, so $a = -9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ even at the exact peak.
top_trap.useWhen: a question asks for velocity and acceleration at the highest point of a vertical throw.
top_trap.example: At $t = 2\text{ s}$ in our problem: $v = 0\text{ m/s}$, $a = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ downward.

symmetry.title: Up-and-down symmetry
symmetry.body: With [no_air:no air drag], a vertical throw is symmetric around its peak: the time to rise equals the time to fall back to the same height ($t_{\text{down}} = t_{\text{up}}$), and at any height the downward speed equals the upward speed ($v_{\text{return}} = -u$).
symmetry.useWhen: an object returns to its launch height (or passes the same height twice).
symmetry.example: Thrown up at $+19.6\text{ m/s}$, it returns to the hand $4\text{ s}$ later at $-19.6\text{ m/s}$.

sections.title: One acceleration for every falling body
sections.body:
{free_fall|Free fall} does not mean *only* dropping something from rest. A ball thrown straight up, a coin dropped from a balcony, and a stone thrown downward are all in free fall the instant they leave your hand — as long as [no_air:air resistance is negligible].

Because {weight|weight} is proportional to mass, mass cancels out of Newton's second law and every object accelerates downward at the same constant [g:$g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$]. That means free fall is simply {suvat|uniform acceleration} turned vertical.

sections.title: Four rules of vertical free fall
sections.note: take upward as the positive y-direction throughout this lesson

rows.note: points downward on the way up, at the peak, and on the way down
watch out for {top_trap|the peak trap}: gravity never switches off
{symmetry|up-and-down symmetry} holds whenever [no_air:air drag is negligible]

rows.text: {disp|Displacement} $y$ is measured from launch, not total path length
rows.note: returning to your hand gives $y = 0$, even though total distance is $2h_{\max}$

sections.title: Worked problem
sections.body:
A ball is thrown straight upward from ground level at [u:$u = 19.6\text{ m/s}$]. Neglecting [no_air:air resistance] and using [g:$g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$]:

Find (1) the [t_up:time to reach the peak], (2) the [h_max:maximum height], (3) the [t_total:total flight time] before it returns to ground level, and (4) its velocity right as it lands.

sections.title: Plan
sections.note: choose upward as positive so u = +19.6 m/s and a = -9.8 m/s²

routes.title: Route A: upward positive, use peak condition $v = 0$
routes.why: One sign convention handles the entire trip smoothly: $y = ut - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$ automatically tracks both climb and fall.
routes.whyNot: Nothing. Keep $a = -9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ everywhere and the algebra does the bookkeeping.

routes.title: Route B: switch $g$ to $+9.8$ at the top and forget signs
routes.path: use $a = -9.8$ going up and $+9.8$ going down in one formula
routes.why: People think gravity slows the ball going up and speeds it up coming down, so $g$ must change sign.
routes.whyNot: Gravity always points **downward**; switching the sign of $a$ mid-problem breaks a single coordinate axis and causes sign errors.

routes.title: Route C: set total distance equal to zero on landing
routes.why: The ball starts and ends at ground level.
routes.whyNot: Distance travelled is $2h_{\max} = 39.2\text{ m}$; only the **displacement** $y$ returns to $0$.

sections.notUsed: Not used: mass of the ball. In {free_fall|free fall}, mass cancels completely.

sections.title: Work it through
sections.note: upward is positive, so u = +19.6 m/s and a = -g = -9.8 m/s²

steps.move: Find the [t_up:climb time] by setting [v_top:velocity to zero] at the peak.
steps.why: With {acceleration|acceleration} $-9.8\text{ m/s}^2$, the ball loses $9.8\text{ m/s}$ of upward speed each second, reaching $0$ after $2\text{ s}$.
steps.whyNot: Do not stop here if the question asks for total flight time — $2\text{ s}$ is only the climb.

steps.why: This uses only [u:$u$], [g:$g$], and [v_top:$v_{\text{top}} = 0$]. Check with $y = ut - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$: $19.6(2) - 4.9(4) = 39.2 - 19.6 = 19.6\text{ m}$.
steps.whyNot: Do not compute $u \times t_{\text{up}} = 39.2\text{ m}$: the ball is slowing down, so average upward speed is $19.6/2 = 9.8\text{ m/s}$.

steps.move: Find the [t_total:total flight time] by setting displacement $y = 0$ at ground level.
steps.why: The two roots are $t = 0\text{ s}$ (launch) and $T = 4\text{ s}$ (landing), confirming {symmetry|$T = 2t_{\text{up}}$}.
steps.whyNot: Do not cancel $T$ blindly without noting that $T = 0$ is the launch instant.

steps.why: The magnitude matches [u:$u = 19.6\text{ m/s}$], and the minus sign shows it is moving **downward**.
steps.whyNot: Do not write $v = 0\text{ m/s}$ for landing velocity: the ball reaches $0$ only *after* hitting the ground, which is no longer {free_fall|free fall}.

sections.title: Height vs. time parabola
sections.note: drag the launch speed u and watch how the peak height grows as u² while flight time grows linearly with u (g = 9.8 m/s²)

sections.title: Check yourself
items: **Peak check**: at the highest point [v_top:$v_{\text{top}} = 0$], yet [g:$a = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$] downward ({top_trap|never zero}).
**Mass independence**: with [no_air:no air drag], a $10\text{ kg}$ rock and a $0.1\text{ kg}$ pebble dropped together hit the ground at the same instant.
**Quadratic height**: doubling [u:$u$] doubles [t_total:$T$] but makes [h_max:$h_{\max}$] **four times** larger (try $u = 9.8$ vs $19.6$ on the plot: $4.9\text{ m}$ vs $19.6\text{ m}$).
**Landing velocity**: in {free_fall|free fall} questions, *velocity when it hits the ground* means the velocity the instant **before** impact, not $0$.
**Symmetry**: returning to launch height takes [t_total:$T = 2t_{\text{up}}$] and arrives with velocity of magnitude $u$ downward.

sections.title: Recall
sections.note: use g = 9.8 m/s² and neglect air resistance

questions.q: A ball is thrown straight upward and reaches its highest point. At that exact instant, what are its velocity $v$ and acceleration $a$?
questions.why: Velocity momentarily equals zero as direction reverses, but gravity stays on, so $a = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ downward ({top_trap|peak trap}).

questions.q: A stone is dropped from rest off a bridge ($g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$). How far does it fall in $t = 3\text{ s}$?
questions.why: With $u = 0$, $h = \frac{1}{2}gt^2 = \frac{1}{2}(9.8)(3^2) = 4.9 \times 9 = 44.1\text{ m}$. Note that $29.4\text{ m/s}$ is the speed, and $88.2\text{ m}$ forgets the $\frac{1}{2}$.

questions.q: Inside a vacuum tube, a $5\text{ kg}$ iron ball and a $0.05\text{ kg}$ rubber ball are released together from the same height. Which lands first?
options: The $5\text{ kg}$ ball, because Earth pulls $100$ times harder on it
Both land at the exact same instant, because both fall with acceleration $g$
The $0.05\text{ kg}$ ball, because it has less inertia to overcome
questions.why: The heavier ball has $100$ times more {weight|weight} and $100$ times more mass, so $a = mg/m = g$ is identical for both.

questions.q: A ball is thrown straight up at $u = 14.7\text{ m/s}$ ($g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$). How long does it take to return to the thrower's hand?
questions.why: Climb time is $t_{\text{up}} = 14.7 / 9.8 = 1.5\text{ s}$. By {symmetry|up-and-down symmetry}, the return trip takes another $1.5\text{ s}$, giving $T = 3.0\text{ s}$.
